title: The Lord of the Rings Game Movie — Gollum, Talion and Minas Ithil
description: Superhero FXL Games brings Gollum's uneasy survival and Talion's defence of Minas Ithil into a two-hour cinematic game-movie compilation. Our review examines its divided loyalties, contrasting voices and the limits of joining separate Middle-earth game stories.
seo_title: Lord of the Rings Game Movie Review: Gollum to Minas Ithil
seo_description: Review this Lord of the Rings game-movie compilation: Gollum, Talion, Shelob and the fall of Minas Ithil, with story, voice and music context explained.
seo_tags: The Lord of the Rings Gollum
review_text:
🏰 Middle-earth storytelling and narrative structure

Superhero FXL Games labels this upload a game movie, and that distinction matters. Its two-hour running time brings together game storytelling associated with The Lord of the Rings: Gollum and Middle-earth: Shadow of War. It is a cinematic game-movie compilation, not an official Peter Jackson theatrical release or a newly released 2025 Tolkien film. The year in the uploader's title identifies the upload's presentation, rather than the release year of the underlying games.

The source chapters and captions reveal two different centres of attention. The earlier material follows Gollum through captivity, evasions and uneasy encounters with Elves; the later material turns towards Talion, Celebrimbor and the threatened city of Minas Ithil. That movement creates a useful contrast between surviving at the margins of power and trying to direct a war. It also needs a little care from the viewer: these games offer separate adaptations, and placing their scenes together does not make them one continuous official storyline.

🕷️ Gollum, Shelob and the atmosphere of mistrust

Gollum's divided impulses give the first part a different kind of tension from the military story that follows. The captions move between concealment, fear of discovery and fixation on the missing Ring. Encounters involving captivity and the Candle Man make vulnerability central to this material. Gollum is interesting here because his dependence on stronger figures never quite removes his capacity to deceive them. Sympathy and suspicion have to remain in the same frame of reference.

Shelob changes the terms of that uncertainty in the Shadow of War material. The game's character biography establishes that she trades Celebrimbor's release for the New Ring and offers Talion visions. The compilation's later captions support that bargain and the argument it creates. She has information Talion needs, but accepting her guidance means accepting that another character controls what he is allowed to know. Her role belongs to this game's interpretation of Middle-earth; it should not be treated as a direct explanation of her role in Tolkien's novel or Jackson's films.

⚔️ Talion, Celebrimbor and the siege of Minas Ithil

The strongest dramatic question in the later story is whether the people defending the city matter as much as the object hidden within it. Talion wants to protect the Gondorians. Celebrimbor repeatedly presses for the Palantír, the seeing-stone that could strengthen their position against Sauron. Their disagreement is more revealing than a simple division between courage and cowardice: both recognise the threat, but they assign a different value to the lives immediately in front of them.

Castamir and his daughter Idril make that argument personal. The source captions trace the defenders' lack of relief, concern for Castamir, and the eventual accusation of betrayal. His bargain with the Witch-king gives the seeing-stone a human cost. A commander trying to preserve what he loves can become part of the machinery destroying his own city. Minas Ithil is the city at issue here; this is distinct from the siege of Minas Tirith in The Return of the King. The distinction helps the fall of the city remain this game's tragedy rather than a confused retelling of the films.

🗣️ Character voices and dramatic performances

The voice credits need to follow the source game, rather than treating every appearance of Gollum as the same performance. Troy Baker plays Talion and Alastair Duncan plays Celebrimbor in Shadow of War; Pollyanna McIntosh plays Shelob. Liam O'Brien is credited as Gollum in that game, while Wayne Forester voices Gollum in Daedalic's The Lord of the Rings: Gollum. Andy Serkis's film performance should not be substituted for either game credit. These are underlying-game credits, not a claim that the uploader commissioned a new cast.

The characters' competing aims provide a useful way to read the dialogue. Talion argues from immediate obligations, Celebrimbor from strategic advantage, and Shelob from a position that withholds certainty. Gollum's speech pulls attention back towards personal need and self-preservation. A compilation depends heavily on those distinctions because the viewer cannot discover the characters through hours of play. They give the conversations purpose even when the surrounding mission structure has been shortened.

🎶 Music, sound design and battlefield immersion

The supplied listening notes describe orchestral strings and brass, choral passages, Gollum's muttering, enclosed ambience and the effects of battle. Read alongside the captions, those notes suggest why this material can sustain attention beyond its dialogue: intimate threat and public catastrophe ask for different scales of sound. A whispered exchange and a city under attack should not carry the same dramatic weight. The contrast is more useful to this review than an unsupported claim that every transition or recording is flawless.

For the underlying Shadow of War score, the composers are Nathan Grigg and Garry Schyman. Their GDC presentation explains the work as music designed for an expansive, changing game world. A linear game-movie edit inevitably changes that relationship: music originally responding to play becomes part of a fixed sequence. The supplied audio observations are not an independent technical assessment of this upload's mix, and individual tracks have not been matched cue by cue. There is no basis here for crediting the compilation's entire soundtrack to Howard Shore or assuming it uses the theatrical films' score.

🎬 How the game-movie format works for viewers

The format offers an accessible route into the characters for someone who wants the narrative without completing the games. Captions and chapter divisions make the movement from Gollum's predicament to the Ranger's conflict easier to follow. The cost is that a game conveys meaning through decisions, repetition and the time spent moving through its world. A film-like edit can retain a conversation while losing the experience that made it matter to the player.

That limitation is especially relevant to Shadow of War's Nemesis System, which builds personal histories between players and enemies. A fixed compilation presents one selected sequence, not the full range of possible encounters. The closing material also moves towards Carnán and the threat associated with the Balrog Tar Goroth, extending the story's concerns beyond the fallen city. It is better approached as a selected journey through game narratives than a promise to contain every mission, ending or strand of Middle-earth history.

🧭 A balanced verdict

The appeal of this compilation lies in the contrast between Gollum's small, anxious calculations and the larger calculations made by Talion, Celebrimbor and Castamir. Across those scales, the recurring question is what someone will surrender for safety or power. That gives the material a stronger point of connection than the shared franchise name alone. The siege storyline supplies the clearest dramatic focus, while Gollum's material offers a more uneasy, personal route into the same world.

Viewers already comfortable with game cinematics are likely to find that combination easier to navigate than someone expecting a conventional standalone film. The change between adaptations, the missing player context and the incomplete scope of the wider stories remain real limitations. Treat it as an introduction to, or revisit of, Middle-earth game storytelling, with substantial plot spoilers. This review uses the source's chapters and captions, supplied viewing and listening notes, and checked game background; it does not claim a continuous independent viewing or a measurement of the upload's audio quality.
